summary: Teach that a solution to a pair of simultaneous linear equations is an (x, y) pair that satisfies BOTH equations at once. When the two lines cross, there is exactly one such pair: the point where the lines meet. The conceptual core is simultaneity: each equation alone has infinitely many solutions (its whole line), so a pair that fits only one equation is not a solution. Learners generate pairs fitting one equation, add a second equation, discover only the crossing works for both, and verify by substituting back into each. Edge cases: distinct parallel lines (no solution) and coincident lines (infinitely many).
misconceptions: Uses only one equation — offers any pair that fits one equation as 'the solution', ignoring the second.
Reads the solution as where a single line crosses an axis, rather than where the two lines meet each other.
Gives only one value (x or y) instead of the pair.
Trusts an inaccurately plotted intersection without checking it by substitution.

activities.title: One equation has many answers; two equations share only one
steps: Take a single equation, e.g. y = x + 1, and list several pairs that satisfy it: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (10,11). Confirm there are infinitely many such pairs — together they form the line.
Now add a second equation, e.g. y = 2x − 1. For each of your pairs from the first list, test whether it also satisfies the second equation.
Find the one pair that satisfies BOTH. Check (2,3): 3 = 2+1 ✓ and 3 = 2×2−1 = 3 ✓. Check (4,5): 5 = 4+1 ✓ but 5 ≠ 2×4−1 = 7 ✗.
State the solution as the PAIR x = 2, y = 3, not a single number.
Plot both lines on one set of axes and mark the intersection; confirm it matches the pair that passed both substitution tests.
activities.insight: A solution to one linear equation alone is any of infinitely many pairs on its line; when the two lines are neither parallel nor the same line (as here), 'solving simultaneously' narrows this to the one pair shared with the second equation, which graphically is where the two lines cross.

activities.title: Slide a point and watch both conditions
steps: Place a point anywhere on the first line and check it against both equations. On the first line it will satisfy equation 1 but (usually) fail equation 2.
Move the point along the first line; equation 1 stays satisfied while equation 2 keeps failing — until exactly at the crossing of the two lines, where both equations are satisfied together.
Record the coordinates of that crossing and substitute them into each equation to verify both are true.

Optionally, if using an interactive tool: edit or drag the two lines; a checker can substitute any chosen (x, y) into both equations, lighting one panel green per satisfied equation and red per failed one, so the moment both go green at once is visible.
activities.insight: Satisfying both equations is a condition a pair either meets or doesn't; only at the intersection do both hold simultaneously, which is why that single point is the solution.

activities.title: Read a graph, then verify by substitution
steps: Given two lines plotted on the same axes, read off the coordinates of the intersection point.
Substitute the read-off pair into BOTH equations. If it fits exactly, that is your solution.

If a rough or poorly scaled graph gives, say, (2.2, 3.1) and substitution does not come out exactly true, refine your reading or solve algebraically (by substitution or elimination). Some intersections have non-integer or fractional coordinates that cannot be read exactly from a graph, so treat the graphical read as approximate until confirmed algebraically.

Distinguish 'where a single line crosses an axis' (an intercept of one equation) from 'where the two lines cross each other' (the solution of both) — mark the meeting point of the two lines, not an axis crossing.
activities.insight: A graphical intersection gives the solution, but an inaccurately plotted graph can mislead, so the read-off pair must be checked by substituting into both equations; the solution is where the two lines meet each other, not where one line meets an axis.

activities.title: When lines don't cross once: no solution or infinitely many
steps: Examine a pair of parallel lines (e.g. y = x + 1 and y = x + 4). Try to find a pair satisfying both; note that the lines have the same slope and never meet, so there is no solution.
Examine two equations that draw the exact same line (coincident lines). Note that every point on the line satisfies both, so there are infinitely many solutions.
Classify given systems into three categories: exactly one solution (lines cross), no solution (parallel), infinitely many (coincident).
Connect this to algebra: relate the graphical categories to substitution or elimination leading to a contradiction (no solution) or an identity (infinitely many).
activities.insight: Simultaneity has three outcomes determined by how the lines relate: one shared point, none, or a whole shared line — each has a graphical and an algebraic signature.

activities.title: Check your understanding: which pair works, and why
steps: Decide, for a multiple-choice item, which pair satisfies BOTH given equations, where at least one distractor pair fits only one equation.
Match each given system to its solution point.
Categorise systems as having one, none, or infinitely many solutions by whether the lines cross, are parallel, or coincide.
For each answer, justify it by substituting the chosen pair into both equations.
activities.insight: Recognising and justifying the correct pair consolidates that only a pair satisfying both equations counts as a solution.

checkQuestion: Two lines are drawn on the same axes: y = x + 1 and y = 2x − 1, and they cross at one point. A pupil says: 'The solution is x = 4, y = 5, because those numbers fit y = x + 1.' Is the pupil right? What IS the solution to the pair of equations, and how do you know?
checkAnswer: The pupil is wrong. x = 4, y = 5 satisfies y = x + 1 (5 = 4 + 1) but NOT y = 2x − 1 (2×4 − 1 = 7, not 5). The solution is the pair that fits BOTH equations — the intersection point x = 2, y = 3 (3 = 2 + 1 ✓ and 3 = 2×2 − 1 ✓). You know because only the point the two lines share satisfies both equations at once.
